The two waves superpose at point P.
What is the resultant displacement at time 0.38 s?

B

hints: Draw a vertical line up from $0.38\text{ s}$ on the time axis and read where it cuts each displacement-time curve in $\text{cm}$.
Recall the principle of superposition at fixed point P: resultant displacement equals the algebraic sum of the two separate displacements, keeping positive and negative signs.

Check the sign of each curve at $0.38\text{ s}$: one curve is just above zero before its $0.40\text{ s}$ zero crossing and the other is well below zero, so decide whether the sum must be small positive or about $-1\text{ cm}$.
walkthrough: Identify the two curves at point P: one starts at $0\text{ cm}$ with amplitude $2.0\text{ cm}$, the other starts near $+1.4\text{ cm}$ with amplitude about $1.6\text{ cm}$.
State the rule: by the principle of superposition, resultant displacement $x = x_1 + x_2$, where $x_1$ and $x_2$ are the separate displacements in $\text{cm}$ with sign.
Read the graph at time $t = 0.38\text{ s}$, just before $0.40\text{ s}$: the $2.0\text{ cm}$ amplitude wave is falling through near zero, so $x_1 \approx +0.3\text{ cm}$.
Read the second wave at the same time: it passed zero near $0.26\text{ s}$ and is approaching its trough, so $x_2 \approx -1.3\text{ cm}$.
Add algebraically: $x \approx (+0.3) + (-1.3) = -1.0\text{ cm}$, with the negative sign showing net displacement below equilibrium.

A.explanation: This would be the magnitude of the sum but with the wrong sign, ignoring that the larger contribution at $0.38\text{ s}$ is negative.

B.explanation: At $0.38\text{ s}$ the two displacements are about $+0.3\text{ cm}$ and $-1.3\text{ cm}$, whose vector sum is about $-1.0\text{ cm}$.

C.explanation: This adds the magnitudes as if both waves were positive, ignoring that one displacement is below the time axis at $0.38\text{ s}$.

D.explanation: This treats both contributions as near maximum negative, but one wave is still slightly positive just before $0.40\text{ s}$.
